newsitem.title: Cambodia: Cambodian PM Ranariddh denies Pol Pot found.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM Ranariddh denies Pol Pot found.

text.p: Cambodia's Co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Thursday Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot had not been found, contradicting a radio report apparently from a rebel splinter group saying he had surrendered.
Ranariddh said most of Pol Pot's supporters had deserted him. They were now trying to find the man reviled by millions of Cambodians and bring him to justice, so far without success, he added.

"Pol Pot has not been found," Ranariddh told reporters at Phnom Penh airport where he was greeting Queen Monineath Sihanouk upon her return from Beijing, where her husband King Sihanouk has been getting medical treatment.
International concern over stability in Cambodia mounted on Thursday with Australia warning that escalating political violence could threaten aid to the impoverished country.

In Washington, a State Department spokesman said U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had to decide whether or not to make a planned trip to Cambodia next week in view of the growing concerns about security. In Phnom Penh, foreign envoys led by U.S. Ambassador Kenneth Quinn urged the government to take steps to control the two premiers' security forces after a fatal clash between the two and to prevent further violence.

"Some of them suggested that one thing may be for the prime ministers to reduce their bodyguards to avoid unnecessary clashes or incidents," Foreign Minister Ung Huot told reporters after a meeting with the ambassadors.
One of the ambassadors at the talks said Quinn had also urged the two premiers to pull some of their bodyguards out of the capital in the interests of maintaining calm.

Pol Pot, one of this century's most notorious figures, fled the Khmer Rouge's Anlong Veng stronghold in the northwest of the country earlier this month after killing his defence chief and 10 members of his family.
Ranariddh said all but between five and 10 of Pol Pot's supporters had deserted him and his former comrades were now hunting him down.
"The other side is not only ready to cut themselves from Pol Pot but to try to capture Pol Pot and send him to an international court," he said.
A radio broadcast apparently made by Pol Pot's former comrades-in-arms on Wednesday said the leader of the 1975-79 'killing fields' regime had turned himself in to them to "confess".
More than one million Cambodians died as a result of overwork, starvation and execution under the Pol Pot government.

Political analysts said the surrender of Pol Pot would likely intensify bitter rivalry between Ranariddh and co-premier Hun Sen as his departure from the scene would clear the way for either of the premiers to strike a deal with the more moderate remnants of the Khmer Rouge.
The two premiers have been feuding for months over power sharing in their coalition as both men seek to bolster their strength in the run-up to elections next year.
"The entry of the Khmer Rouge could change the balance of forces," an Asian diplomat said.
On Tuesday night two men were killed as bodyguards loyal to the two premiers fought a gun battle on the streets of Phnom Penh after a dispute flared.

Both premiers maintain security units of more than 1,000 heavily-armed men in the vicinity of the capital and political analysts say the danger is that a clash between the two forces could spin out of control and draw in units from the armed forces.
"There are so many armed people around and some of them are trigger happy," another diplomat said.
